newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- Long end to lead flattening.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- Long end to lead flattening.

text.p: Now that this week's deluge of supply is over, the U.S. Treasury yield curve's recent steepening trend should come to an end, analysts said on Friday.

"I suspect the market will do better and the curve will flatten back out," said Scott Graham, co-head bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "The market should pop up to quarter-end as cash finds its way off the sidelines."
"The fundamentals of the market have not changed," he said. "The market is in pretty good shape."

The spread between the two-year note and 30-year bond widened to its highest point in a month on Friday morning at 75 basis points, up from 66 basis points late Monday and 73 at Thursday's close. The curve had not been so wide since a spread of 76 basis points on May 27.
The 75-basis-point spread was well above the five-day and 10-day averages of about 69 basis points, and at the top of the 90-day range of 60 to 76 basis points.

In contrast to typical curve movements, the steepening of the yield curve this week was not due to expectations of Federal Reserve policy, but rather the heavy corporate issuance, since much of the new issuance was in longer-dated paper.
That forced some portfolios to sell Treasuries -- as well as mortgage-backed and other corporates -- to make room for the new supply.
In all, some $5.5 billion in investment grade debt was issued, including a $2.8 billion multi-tranche deal from the State of New Jersey, which jolted the market on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the Treasury sold $27.0 billion in two- and five-year notes, largely taken down by dealers.
As a result of the huge amount of supply, the 30-year bond jumped to a high of 6.79 percent from 6.66 percent earlier this week, while the two-year note edged up to 6.05 percent from 6.00 percent.
"The front end is acting like an anchor right now with the long end swinging both ways," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.
The two-year still faces the problem of being so tight to the federal funds rate, giving it little room to move on the upside.
Plus, analysts noted that much of the so-called quarter-end window dressing buying is going into the short end.

"The market is settling into a little bit of a range," said Matthew Alexy, chief Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "So, I don't expect a (major) yield curve movement until Thursday (when the June employment report will be released)."
Instead, players said the curve should just go back to where it was last week, with the long bond heading back down to around the 6.66 percent area and the two-year note to near 6.00 percent.
"People will start to buy back their hedges (from the corporate issues) and that will lead to a flatter curve," Graham said.

Meanwhile, fundamentals should aid the flattening, as upcoming economic data -- beginning with employment -- is expected to be on the strong side. That, analysts said, would put the fear of a rate hike back into play and consequently push up the two-year note's yield.

"Everyone is in agreement that the Fed will not do anything next week," said one head trader at a primary dealer, referring to the Fed's policy setting meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday. "But there is no agreement whether they will raise rates later."
